lesson.title: Is the Difference Real? Testing Two Independent Means
lesson.summary: The two-sample t-test asks whether an observed difference between two independent sample means is more than what random sampling variation alone would produce, reusing the same standard error built for the two-sample t-interval.
lesson.body:
A confidence interval estimates how big a difference is. A hypothesis test asks a sharper question: is there convincing evidence of any difference at all? The two-sample t-test borrows its standard error directly from the two-sample t-interval, then plugs it into the same general test statistic pattern from the one-sample t-test: (statistic minus hypothesized parameter) divided by standard error. Here the parameter is mu1 minus mu2, and almost always the hypothesized value is 0, meaning no difference between the two population means.

So the hypotheses are typically written H0: mu1 equals mu2 (equivalently mu1 minus mu2 equals 0), against an alternative that is either two-sided (mu1 does not equal mu2) or one-sided in whichever direction the research question points. The test statistic is t equals (xbar1 minus xbar2) divided by the square root of (s1 squared over n1 plus s2 squared over n2), with the same conservative degrees of freedom used for the interval.

Worked example. A researcher wants to know whether caffeine speeds up reaction time. Ten participants take caffeine, ten take a placebo, assigned at random. Caffeine group: n1 equals 10, mean reaction time 250 milliseconds, standard deviation 20. Placebo group: n2 equals 10, mean 270 milliseconds, standard deviation 25. Hypotheses: H0: mu_caffeine equals mu_placebo, Ha: mu_caffeine is less than mu_placebo (caffeine lowers average reaction time). The standard error is the square root of (400 divided by 10) plus (625 divided by 10), which is the square root of 40 plus 62.5, or the square root of 102.5, about 10.124. The test statistic is (250 minus 270) divided by 10.124, which is negative 20 divided by 10.124, about negative 1.98. Conservative degrees of freedom is the smaller of 9 and 9, so df equals 9. The one-tailed critical value at alpha equals 0.05 with df equals 9 is 1.833. Since the size of our test statistic, 1.98, exceeds 1.833, the result falls in the rejection region. Checking the t-table more closely, at df equals 9 the value 1.833 corresponds to a tail area of 0.05 and 2.262 corresponds to 0.025, and our statistic sits between those, so the p-value is between 0.025 and 0.05, roughly 0.04. Since that p-value is below a significance level of 0.05, we reject H0. There is convincing evidence that mean reaction time is lower for the caffeine group than for the placebo group.

The conditions are the same ones needed for the interval: random assignment or random sampling for each group, independence within and between the two groups, and either roughly normal population shapes or samples large enough to lean on the Central Limit Theorem. With only 10 observations per group here, it would be worth checking a dotplot of each group for strong skew or outliers before trusting the result, a judgment call the robustness section later in this chapter will make more precise.
